paragraphs: A visual model can recognize image content without consistently understanding the same scene from different viewpoints. This paper addresses that gap by training vision foundation models on videos, where changes across frames provide information about three-dimensional structure. The approach, called 3DPoV, uses self-supervision to make visual features more consistent as the viewpoint changes.

Its first component finds corresponding points across video frames and encourages consistency between their nearest neighbors in feature space. A second component uses a reference to guide the ordering of image patches, requiring their representations to remain aligned as well as informative. The authors also assemble a mixture of video datasets suited to these objectives. Together, these components make relationships across frames central to learning.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results for matching keypoints across viewpoints, estimating depth, and estimating surface normals. It also reports consistent improvements across several model backbones, including DINOv3. These findings support using temporal correspondence and patch alignment to strengthen the geometric information available in general-purpose visual representations.
icml-2026-3dpov-improving-3d-understandi.tldr: 3DPoV uses correspondence and patch alignment across video frames to improve vision models’ understanding of three-dimensional structure.

paragraphs: Many useful statistics depend on relationships among observations rather than on individual observations alone. A U-statistic averages a function over groups of a fixed size, called its degree. Degree-two examples include Kendall’s correlation coefficient, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and the Gini mean difference. This paper studies their computation when data are distributed in a federated setting.

The proposed protocol supports degree two and higher by combining multiparty computation with central differential privacy. Multiparty computation supplies the secure computation component, while differential privacy supplies the privacy guarantee for the statistical result. This addresses shortcomings of earlier approaches that either use the lower-utility local privacy model or scale poorly with domain discretization.

The authors analyze accuracy, communication requirements, and computational cost, then evaluate the protocol empirically. They report substantially improved accuracy, including reductions in mean squared error of up to four orders of magnitude for Kendall’s coefficient compared with existing baselines. That example demonstrates the potential accuracy benefit of the combined protocol without implying an identical improvement for every statistic.
icml-2026-accurate-private-secure-federa.tldr: A secure federated protocol computes higher-degree U-statistics with central differential privacy and substantially better reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Language-model pretraining involves choices about both the model’s capacity and the order of its training data. Curriculum-Guided Layer Scaling connects these choices: it gradually adds layers while moving training toward more difficult material. The goal is compute-efficient learning through coordination between model growth and the demands of the examples being presented.

At the 100-million-parameter scale, the curriculum begins with synthetic short stories and transitions to general web text. The resulting models outperform baseline methods on PIQA and ARC question answering. At the 1.2-billion-parameter scale, the authors use a DistilBERT-based classifier to organize DataComp-LM into a progression from general text toward technical or specialized content.

The reported results associate this coordinated increase in depth and data difficulty with better generalization and zero-shot performance across downstream benchmarks. The contribution is a training framework that gives progressive layer stacking a matching data curriculum. Its findings support the usefulness of growing capacity alongside task difficulty for the evaluated knowledge-intensive and reasoning tasks.
icml-2026-curriculum-guided-layer-scalin.tldr: Coordinating gradual model growth with increasingly difficult training text improves reported language-model generalization.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models offer an alternative to autoregressive text generation, but their backbone can make inference expensive. The paper identifies quadratic attention costs and key-value cache overhead as obstacles in Transformer-based designs. DiffuMamba addresses this by combining a masked diffusion objective with a bidirectional Mamba backbone that models sequences in linear time.

The authors also introduce DiffuMamba-H, which interleaves attention with the Mamba components. Across model sizes up to 1.3 billion parameters, both variants match the downstream performance of Transformer-based diffusion models. On long sequences, the reported peak inference-throughput improvements are 8.2 times for DiffuMamba and 4.3 times for the hybrid variant.

Beyond these models, the paper compares modern diffusion language-model strategies using both complexity analysis and measured efficiency. Within that comparison, cache-efficient block diffusion using Mamba mixers is the only strategy that scales linearly with sequence length and delivers the strongest performance across the baselines. This points to the combination of backbone and generation strategy as an important direction for efficient diffusion-based text generation.
icml-2026-diffumamba-high-throughput-dif.tldr: DiffuMamba replaces Transformer-heavy diffusion backbones with Mamba to increase long-sequence throughput while matching reported downstream performance.

paragraphs: Diffusion Flow Matching is a generative modeling framework whose convergence guarantees remain incompletely understood. This paper studies versions based on Brownian motion, concentrating on discretization error: the discrepancy introduced when a continuous process is implemented through discrete steps. Its contribution is theoretical, providing bounds on how that error affects the generated distribution.

The first analysis measures distributional discrepancy using Kullback–Leibler divergence. Under finite-moment conditions and a mild integrability assumption on the score, the authors obtain bounds with improved dependence on dimension relative to previous work. Dimension dependence matters because it describes how the guarantee changes as the number of modeled coordinates grows. The authors characterize their scaling as state of the art to their knowledge under minimal conditions.

The second analysis uses the 2-Wasserstein distance, another measure of distributional discrepancy. It requires an additional first-order score integrability assumption and weak log-concavity. Under those conditions, the dimension dependence agrees with the KL analysis. These results strengthen the mathematical understanding of discretized Brownian-motion-based DFM while explicitly tying each guarantee to its assumptions.
icml-2026-diffusion-flow-matching-dimens.tldr: The paper derives improved dimension-dependent discretization bounds for Brownian-motion-based Diffusion Flow Matching under stated regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Multi-objective combinatorial optimization searches a huge discrete space for solutions that offer different tradeoffs among competing goals. The number of possible combinations can grow exponentially, making direct exploration difficult. This paper turns the search into an online learning problem by decomposing decisions into smaller parts and constructing complete solutions sequentially.

Each position is handled through a bandit subproblem, with adaptive guidance from experts during construction. This decomposition supports a regret bound of O(d√(T log T)), where d measures subproblem dimensionality. The bound depends on that smaller dimensionality rather than the size of the full combinatorial space, providing a theoretical reason to study this construction strategy.

On standard benchmarks, the method reaches 80–98% of specialized solvers’ performance while improving sample and computational efficiency over Bayesian optimization by two to three orders of magnitude. In AI accelerator hardware-software co-design, it also outperforms competing methods under fixed simulation budgets. The reported advantage grows with problem scale and the number of objectives, supporting decomposed bandit search for expensive optimization.
icml-2026-divide-and-learn-multi-objecti.tldr: Decomposing combinatorial search into sequential bandit decisions yields theoretical regret guarantees and strong reported efficiency across multiple objectives.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning represents scenes in terms of objects, with the aim of supporting compositional generalization and robustness to unfamiliar data. Yet identifying objects does not by itself establish that their representations support useful reasoning. This paper examines an evaluation gap: existing benchmarks often emphasize object discovery or simple classification probes rather than the broader goals of object-centric learning.

The authors propose using instruction-tuned vision-language models as evaluators. Across visual question-answering datasets, these evaluators measure how effectively object-centric representations can support more complex reasoning. This makes representation usefulness a direct focus of evaluation and provides a way to benchmark it across diverse question-answering settings.

A second contribution is a task and metric that assess localization and representation usefulness together. Jointly evaluating where an object is and what its representation supports addresses inconsistencies from measuring those properties separately. The paper also supplies a simple baseline based on reconstructing multiple features. Its central contribution is therefore a broader evaluation framework for assessing what object-centric representations actually enable.
icml-2026-evaluating-object-centric-mode.tldr: The paper proposes evaluating object-centric representations through complex visual reasoning and a joint measure of localization and usefulness.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits are attractive because they permit exact inference with tractable computation. However, their mixture weights do not depend on the data, limiting how well they reflect local geometric structure. This paper investigates whether Voronoi tessellations can introduce that structure directly into the sum nodes where circuit components are combined.

The central difficulty is that a straightforward geometric modification destroys tractability. The authors formalize this incompatibility and develop two responses. One permits approximate inference while guaranteeing lower and upper bounds on the answer. The other identifies a structural condition on the Voronoi tessellation under which exact, tractable inference becomes possible again. The alternatives provide different ways to retain useful computational guarantees.

To make the geometric construction learnable, the paper introduces a differentiable relaxation that supports gradient-based optimization. The resulting approach is evaluated on standard density-estimation tasks. The contribution connects geometric expressiveness with controlled inference: bounds remain available in the approximate setting, while exact computation is recovered under the stated structural condition.
icml-2026-geometry-aware-probabilistic-c.tldr: Voronoi-based probabilistic circuits incorporate local geometry through bounded approximate inference or exact inference under a structural condition.

paragraphs: Spectral approaches to prediction and planning simplify movement using a shared set of mathematical modes. Existing grid-cell and successor-representation theories commonly assume that translations commute, so changing their order does not matter. This paper addresses environments with path-dependent effects, including circulation, rotational drift, and topological loops, where that assumption breaks.

The theory studies directed actions on discrete tori using twisted translation operators. It proves that a twisted Fourier transform organizes the resulting controlled Markov operators into exact blocks. Actions retain a universal harmonic basis, but their effects require small matrices rather than single scalar values. This preserves a shared representation while accommodating the richer structure associated with nontrivial holonomy.

The authors derive closed-form expressions for successor representations and a gauge-invariant principle identifying when environments share predictive structure. They also prove a lower bound showing that nonzero holonomy requires internal representational dimension. Together, these results establish a mathematical foundation for transferring prediction across the studied directed-action environments without learning a separate eigenbasis for each one.
icml-2026-holonomy-grid-codes-for-genera.tldr: A twisted Fourier theory extends grid-based prediction to path-dependent actions and characterizes shared predictive structure across environments.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning depends on sources contributing useful data, but rewarding submitted datasets can create incentives to manipulate them. A source might duplicate observations or add noise to raise its reward or reduce others’ benefits. This paper studies how a reward mechanism for Bayesian models can support both fair collaboration and truthful data submission.

The mechanism combines semivalues, including the Shapley value, with a data valuation function based on a validation set hidden from contributors. Semivalues provide the fairness component. Because their values also depend on other sources’ data, the authors introduce an additional condition for proving that submitting data reflecting a source’s true knowledge maximizes its expected coalition values and semivalues.

The resulting guarantees concern collaborative fairness and incentives for truthfulness at equilibrium. The paper also considers how these goals can be relaxed when the mediator has a limited reward budget or no validation set. Synthetic and real-world experiments support the theoretical analysis. The key contribution is to treat truthful contribution as part of reward design rather than assuming submitted data are already trustworthy.
icml-2026-incentivizing-truthfulness-and.tldr: A Bayesian data-reward mechanism combines fairness with equilibrium incentives for truthful contributions under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Generative policies trained by imitation can perform well, but their behavior is constrained by demonstration coverage and distribution shift. Reinforcement learning can improve them, although updating a large action decoder is often unstable and sample inefficient. Lagrangian Perturbation Diffusion Steering adapts behavior by learning a compact change to the decoder’s noise input while keeping the generative policy frozen.

The method optimizes this perturbation with a Lagrangian trust-region objective. It seeks higher downstream value while restricting departure from the latent prior. This makes the allowed change in noise space an explicit part of optimization. The learned component can therefore steer the existing decoder without requiring updates to its large set of parameters.

Across manipulation, locomotion, and dexterous manipulation benchmarks, the paper reports improved sample efficiency, success, and return, with return gains of up to 25% over prior baselines. It also retains higher action-space entropy than unconstrained noise steering. Evaluations using flow-matching backbones, a large vision-language-action model, and a physical Franka robot demonstrate applicability beyond compact diffusion policies and simulation.
icml-2026-lagrangian-perturbation-diffus.tldr: LP-DS improves frozen generative policies by learning constrained noise-space perturbations, with reported gains in efficiency and control performance.

paragraphs: Brain-network analysis often models connections between pairs of regions, but disease-related patterns can involve groups of regions interacting together. Hypergraphs can represent such group relationships through hyperedges. Existing approaches, however, often fix these groups in advance or learn only their weights, limiting their ability to adapt to structures at different resolutions.

MuHL introduces adaptive learning of hyperedges across multiple scales. It constructs hierarchical node features and uses graph signals at several resolutions to learn higher-order interactions through continuous hyperedge construction. The important change is that the model learns the group structure itself, giving it greater flexibility than methods restricted to adjusting predefined connections.

Experiments across multiple brain-network benchmarks show consistent improvements in disease classification at different stages. The learned hyperedges also identify key brain regions and group interactions associated with disease progression. These findings connect predictive performance with interpretable patterns of connectivity. The reported associations support MuHL’s potential for analyzing neurodegenerative disorders, while the classification results establish its usefulness in the evaluated benchmark settings.
icml-2026-learning-multi-scale-hypergrap.tldr: MuHL learns groups of interacting brain regions at multiple scales, improving disease classification and revealing progression-associated connectivity patterns.

paragraphs: A rule with a short program description may be learnable from few examples, yet finding that program can require an enormous search. Conversely, gradient-based learning can avoid enumerating programs but need exponentially many examples for some program families. This paper investigates whether pretrained language models can supply a useful search bias that bridges these computational and statistical difficulties.

LLM-PV asks a pretrained model to propose candidate programs, executes them, scores them on held-out validation data, and selects the best. The proposal distribution remains fixed: neither gradient updates nor validation feedback changes how candidates are sampled. The language model supplies plausible programs, while execution and validation determine which proposal fits the task.

Across parity variants, pattern matching, and primality testing, the method often recovers the exact rule from a small labeled dataset and generalizes to much longer sequences. Compared methods can fit training examples yet generalize unreliably. These findings suggest that a pretrained model’s program prior can make empirical risk minimization practical without exhaustive enumeration.
icml-2026-llm-priors-for-erm-over-progra.tldr: LLM-PV samples programs from a fixed pretrained language model and selects them by execution, often recovering rules from few examples.

paragraphs: A location’s textual description captures its identity, but human visits provide another signal: how people actually use it. Existing representations often emphasize static metadata or movement patterns tied to particular trajectories. Mobility-Embedded POIs combines language-model embeddings with mobility data to learn representations centered on places and their functions across different users and times.

The framework represents individual visits with temporal context and uses contrastive learning to align them with learnable place embeddings. For locations with few observations, it propagates temporal visiting patterns from nearby, frequently visited places at multiple spatial scales. This mechanism addresses sparse visitation data while retaining a focus on the place rather than a single traveler’s route.

The authors introduce five map-enrichment tasks that assess both identity and function. Adding ME-POIs to text embeddings consistently outperforms text-only and mobility-only baselines across these tasks. Mobility-only training also surpasses text-only models on certain tasks. These results support real-world usage as a valuable complement to descriptions when building general-purpose representations of places.
icml-2026-mobility-embedded-pois-learnin.tldr: ME-POIs combines visit patterns with textual embeddings to represent both what places are and how people use them.

paragraphs: A language model’s earlier conversation can shape its later behavior, including the persistence of tendencies associated with previous hallucinations. This paper introduces History Echoes to investigate how conversational history biases subsequent responses. Its focus is on connecting observable behavioral persistence with the evolution of the model’s internal representations during a conversation.

The framework approaches consistency in two ways. A probabilistic analysis models conversations as Markov chains to quantify whether conversational states persist. A geometric analysis measures consistency between consecutive hidden representations. These views examine the same phenomenon at different levels: patterns in generated behavior and patterns in the internal states that accompany generation.

Across three model families and six datasets covering diverse phenomena, the authors find a strong correlation between the two perspectives. They connect persistent behavior to a geometric trap in which gaps in latent space confine the model’s trajectory. The contribution is an account of how conversational habits appear in representation geometry, giving behavioral persistence a measurable internal counterpart within the studied models and datasets.
icml-2026-old-habits-die-hard-how-conver.tldr: History Echoes links persistent conversational behavior to geometric confinement in language models’ hidden representations.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders seek interpretable features in neural-network activations, but some learned features never activate. This feature death wastes representational capacity and can reintroduce overlapping representations. The paper explains why identical configurations can produce almost no dead features on GPT-2 but more than 70% on AlphaFold3.

The proposed mechanism concerns activation dimensions whose mean magnitude is large relative to their variation across tokens. At initialization, a feature’s alignment with the activation mean shifts its input before activation. Features pointing against that mean can remain negative and never fire. A severity measure based on the ratio of mean and variation norms predicts initial death rates across 454 model-layer combinations spanning several model domains.

Features can revive during training, but recovery requires the autoencoder bias to learn the activation mean, which becomes prohibitively slow when outlier severity is high. Subtracting the mean beforehand avoids that learning problem. Mean-centering eliminates outlier-induced death across all tested models, supporting both the proposed mechanism and a principled explanation for when this preprocessing is needed.
icml-2026-on-the-relationship-between-ac.tldr: Large activation means can cause sparse-autoencoder feature death, and mean-centering removes this cause across the tested models.

paragraphs: Combining noisy human annotations can reduce the cost of obtaining labels, but aggregation may also amplify biases related to sensitive attributes. This paper analyzes fairness in Majority Vote and Optimal Bayesian aggregation using an epsilon-fairness framework based on demographic parity. It asks both how annotator bias affects consensus and how fairness can be enforced afterward.

For small crowds, the authors bound the fairness gap of Majority Vote using the individual annotators’ fairness gaps. They also show that, under interpretable conditions, the consensus fairness gap converges exponentially quickly to the ground-truth fairness gap. This separates agreement with ground truth from demographic fairness: the target labels themselves may still exhibit an unfair gap.

To address that remaining issue, the paper extends a multiclass fairness post-processing algorithm from continuous to discrete settings. The extension enforces strict demographic parity constraints on any aggregation rule. Experiments with synthetic and real datasets support the theoretical findings and the method’s effectiveness, combining an analysis of inherited bias with a mechanism for imposing explicit fairness constraints.
icml-2026-optimal-fair-aggregation-of-cr.tldr: The paper bounds fairness gaps in crowdsourced label aggregation and provides discrete post-processing that enforces demographic parity.

paragraphs: Sampling structured discrete objects from an unnormalized posterior can be approached by learning to construct them step by step. Existing methods use a deterministic Markov decision process whose policy depends on the current construction state. This paper shows that this restriction can hinder the propagation of training signals and severely limit what the learned sampler can express.

The problem arises through state aliasing: the current state can fail to distinguish construction histories that matter for future choices. The proposed method augments the process with learnable latent dynamics, allowing the policy to depend on its full trajectory. This produces path-dependent discrete amortized inference, retaining information about how an object was assembled rather than conditioning only on its present state.

The authors prove that existing learning algorithms for amortized samplers extend to this setting. On standard benchmarks, the resulting method often learns faster and explores the state space more effectively than prior techniques. These findings support trajectory-dependent policies as a way to improve both the expressive capacity and training behavior of discrete samplers.
icml-2026-path-dependent-discrete-amorti.tldr: Giving discrete samplers learned memory of their construction paths addresses state aliasing and often improves learning and exploration.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve language-model reasoning, but a reward delivered only at the end provides a sparse learning signal. Textual criticism can supply richer guidance. This paper argues that useful feedback must do more than describe an error correctly: it should help the receiving model improve its policy when given that feedback in context.

The usefulness of a critic’s advice depends on the actor’s ability to learn from it, creating a coupled optimization problem. The authors formalize this relationship as a Stackelberg bilevel program and derive Bilevel Natural Language Actor-Critic, or Bi-NAC. It jointly trains the critic to produce reward-improving feedback and the actor to make productive use of that feedback.

Across MATH-500, MBPP, and GPQA, Bi-NAC improves sample and parameter efficiency relative to reinforcement-learning and fixed-critic baselines. A 2B model scores 46.6% versus 41.4% for a 3B GRPO baseline on MATH-500; a 6B model scores 49.3% versus 43.6% for a 7B baseline on GPQA. These results support optimizing feedback for its effect on learning.
icml-2026-rl-with-learnable-textual-feed.tldr: Bi-NAC jointly trains a feedback critic and reasoning actor so that textual advice improves learning, with reported efficiency gains.

paragraphs: Language models can suggest convincing research ideas that fail when implemented. This paper investigates whether automated experiments can turn those suggestions into measurable research progress. The authors build an executor that implements ideas and runs parallel GPU experiments, using language-model pretraining and post-training as realistic research environments. It successfully implements a large fraction of ideas sampled from frontier models.

The study compares evolutionary search and reinforcement learning as ways to use execution feedback. Execution-guided evolutionary search finds a post-training method that significantly beats GRPO and a pretraining recipe that beats nanoGPT within ten search epochs. Models often contribute meaningful algorithmic ideas, although their improvement tends to saturate early and scaling trends appear only occasionally.

Reinforcement learning produces a different outcome: average execution reward rises, but the best achievable reward does not improve as models converge on simple ideas. This mode collapse distinguishes improving typical proposals from discovering stronger ones. The study establishes practical feasibility for substantial automated experimentation while identifying different strengths and failure patterns in learning from its results.
icml-2026-towards-execution-grounded-aut.tldr: Automated execution enables productive research search, but evolutionary search and reinforcement learning show different limits in discovering better ideas.

paragraphs: Learned denoisers can help reconstruct images, but guaranteeing stable behavior beyond the training data is difficult. A central requirement is Lipschitz control, which limits how much a network’s output can change when its input changes. This paper constructs a denoising architecture with a global bound of at most one, making it nonexpansive.

The construction uses the action of permutations on the image lattice to constrain the neural architecture. Its guarantee comes from that structure rather than from empirical checks on training examples. The authors then combine the denoiser with forward imaging operators to obtain a reconstruction mechanism that is provably contractive and, as a consequence, globally convergent.

Experiments on standard inverse problems, including superresolution and deblurring, show competitive reconstruction performance relative to softly constrained baselines. The contribution brings together image quality and a mathematical guarantee on the reconstruction process. Nonexpansiveness is established for the denoiser, while contraction is established for the combined mechanism; this distinction explains how the architectural constraint supports convergence of reconstruction.
icml-2026-trainable-nonexpansive-denoise.tldr: A globally nonexpansive denoiser supports provably convergent image reconstruction while delivering competitive reported image quality.

paragraphs: Automated safety evaluations often count how frequently attacks trigger responses that a judge labels harmful. That count treats detected violations as a proxy for real-world harm, even though judges are imperfect and flagged responses differ in operational usefulness. This paper asks whether safety training can influence the kind of failure a model produces when an attack succeeds.

Inspired by security honeypots, the authors construct responses that automated judges frequently flag as harmful but that provide limited practical value for carrying out harm. They use these responses as hard negatives in the safety-training pipeline. The aim is to shift failures toward less actionable content while also reducing harmful behavior overall.

The reported findings show that shaping failure modes can reduce both the frequency of harmful failures and their real-world impact. This makes actionability a useful consideration alongside attack success rates. The contribution is a training approach that addresses the consequences of failed defenses, together with evidence that safety evaluation benefits from distinguishing a judge-detected violation from an operationally useful harmful response.
icml-2026-training-with-honeypots-reshap.tldr: Honeypot-inspired safety training aims to make adversarial failures less actionable while reducing the frequency of harmful responses.

paragraphs: Unsupervised disentanglement seeks latent factors that correspond to distinct concepts without labeled examples of those factors. This paper defines concepts through how they affect observations: locally, different factors should change observations in orthogonal directions. That functional definition shifts attention toward the geometry of the generative mapping and the effects of changing each latent variable.

The authors express this requirement as an orthogonality constraint on the mapping’s Jacobian. They prove that it yields identifiability for general nonlinear generative models without requiring statistical independence or causal assumptions. The result depends on the latent domain admitting every combination of factor values, so the conclusion is tied to both the geometric condition and the domain assumption.

Experiments with orthogonality-regularized normalizing flows support the theory and show reliable recovery of ground-truth factors. The analysis also offers insight into the success of variational autoencoders. The contribution provides an alternative foundation for identifiable unsupervised representations, challenging broad impossibility claims by establishing what becomes possible under these specific structural conditions.
icml-2026-unsupervised-disentanglement-w.tldr: Local orthogonality makes nonlinear latent factors identifiable when the latent domain includes all factor combinations, without independence or causal assumptions.

paragraphs: Generating multiple solutions can improve reasoning only if a system can identify the stronger candidates. This paper finds that models are substantially better at comparing two candidates than at scoring each independently. V1 uses that advantage to unite solution generation and self-verification through pairwise ranking, making verification a central part of inference-time scaling.

V1-Infer organizes comparisons as a tournament and directs verification effort toward pairs whose relative correctness is most uncertain. V1-PairRL jointly trains one model to generate solutions and compare them. Joint training lets the verifier adapt as the generator’s output distribution changes, addressing the connection between what a model produces and what it must learn to judge.

Across coding, agent, mathematical, and medical-question benchmarks, V1-Infer improves Pass@1 by up to 10% over pointwise verification and exceeds state-of-the-art aggregation-based scaling with greater efficiency. V1-PairRL reports test-time scaling gains of 3.8–10 percentage points over standard reinforcement learning and pointwise joint training, plus base Pass@1 gains of up to 8.7 points over standard reinforcement learning.
icml-2026-v1-unifying-generation-and-sel.tldr: V1 improves parallel reasoning through uncertainty-guided pairwise comparisons and joint training of generation and self-verification.

paragraphs: Group emotion recognition aims to infer social dynamics from scenes involving multiple people. Models can take shortcuts by relying on the background instead of the participants’ behavior, producing inaccurate judgments. VIBE addresses this problem with a framework that combines audio, video, and text while organizing their relationships through causal structuring.

The method uses mathematical constraints to separate behavior-related emotion information from background interference. It then adjusts neural attention according to physical synchrony, making the coordination of people’s movements a direct influence on what the model emphasizes. This connects the representation to the group’s observed dynamics rather than allowing the scene context to dominate recognition.

VIBE also projects latent representations into a semantically structured space informed by textual descriptions, connecting visual dynamics with human-interpretable meaning. The paper reports consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in its experiments. Its contribution combines behavior-focused representation learning, synchrony-driven attention, and textual semantic alignment within one framework for recognizing group emotion from multiple modalities.
icml-2026-vibe-disentangling-social-dyna.tldr: VIBE combines behavior-focused multimodal representations, physical synchrony, and textual semantics to improve reported group emotion recognition.
